history.new: Among 13 tail-output quasigroup hashes and 4 cascades, measured against FNV-1a-64, MX64 (multiply-xorshift with the splitmix64 finaliser), BLAKE2b-64 and CRC32 on avalanche, bit independence, chi-square, collisions and throughput, no quasigroup construction improves significantly on the best baseline in any measured dimension (some have numerically smaller maximal bias or bit-independence values, within noise).

history.new: Every tail-output variant fails at least one quality test (forward-only - avalanche; reverse-pass - distribution, 2.4-2.7x bucket collisions and 32,624 full collisions on near-duplicates). The cascades over the random Latin square and the Z/256 isotope match MX64 and BLAKE2b-64 on every quality test run, but are several times slower than BLAKE2b and over 10x slower than numpy-vectorised MX64 in the same run (EXP-C18-05). Throughput figures are load-dependent indicative ranges - the quasigroup variants measured 11-52 MB/s in EXP-C18-04 and 20-98 MB/s on the Skeptic's re-run, the cascades 10-13 and 19-21 MB/s - but the ordering is stable - the fastest quasigroup variant is at least 4x slower than MX64 and 5x slower than FNV-1a in both runs. MX64 is at least as good on every axis within noise. Against FNV-1a alone the good cascades have better avalanche (FNV-1a max bias 0.5); FNV-1a's z = -9.8 on sequential keys means more uniform than random, not a defect. This is not a security evaluation.
history.old: Every tail-output variant fails at least one quality test (forward-only - avalanche; reverse-pass - distribution, 2.4-2.7x bucket collisions and 32,624 full collisions on near-duplicates). The cascades over the random Latin square and the Z/256 isotope match MX64 and BLAKE2b-64 on every quality test run, but at 10-13 MB/s they were about 3x slower than BLAKE2b (one C call per key) and over 10x slower than numpy-vectorised MX64 in the same run (EXP-C18-05; EXP-C18-04 under different load - FNV-1a 640, MX64 428, BLAKE2b 74 MB/s, quasigroup variants 11-52 MB/s). MX64 is at least as good on every axis. Against FNV-1a alone, the good cascades have better avalanche (FNV-1a max bias 0.5) and better distribution on sequential keys (FNV-1a z = -9.8), at a large speed cost. This is not a security evaluation.

limitations: Python/numpy implementations on a shared machine (times indicative); a small subset of SMHasher-style tests; one random Latin square (not uniformly sampled); 16-byte keys for avalanche.
novelty_basis: Quasigroup string processing for cryptographic primitives and pseudo-random generators is established (Markovski et al.; Gligoroski, Candidate one-way functions and one-way permutations based on quasigroup string transformations, https://ia.cr/2005/352; Edon-R); the benchmark against these baselines is ours.
